list.listitem: In women at high risk for pre-eclampsia, calcium supplementation ( A ), low-dose aspirin (starting after 12-weeks gestation, A ), and vitamin D supplementation (in White women and women without obesity, B ) can be considered to reduce the risk of preeclampsia, small for gestational age, and preterm birth.

Screening for hypertension and symptoms of preeclampsia should occur at each prenatal visit. C Although a variety of risk factors, including genetics, are associated with increased probability of preeclampsia, most cases of preeclampsia occur in healthy nulliparous women with no obvious risk factors.

Blood pressures more than 140/90 mmHg, proteinuria 1+ or more, rapid weight gain, or symptoms of headache, vision changes, and epigastric or right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain should prompt evaluation for pre-eclampsia (i.e., CBC with platelets, serum creatinine, LDH, AST and ALT, and 24-hour urine protein). C
Any patient with pre-eclampsia with severe features, HELLP syndrome, or eclampsia should be admitted to a tertiary care hospital for evaluation and management. C

Early delivery for women with early-onset severe preeclampsia appears to reduce neonatal morbidity; for women with preeclampsia without severe features, early planned delivery appears to reduce maternal morbidity but increases neonatal morbidity with no increase in neonatal mortality. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG, 2020) recommends delivery at 37 weeks for stable preeclampsia without severe features and at 34 weeks in preeclampsia with severe features unless other indications for delivery arise or neonatal survival is not anticipated. B
Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis and initial treatment in severe preeclampsia/eclampsia and should be used in labor and up to 24 hours postpartum. A

Although the benefit of antihypertensive treatment for women with mild to moderate hypertension during pregnancy has been of uncertain value,a recent RCT found treatment to a blood pressure target of <140/90 mm/Hg resulted in better maternal outcomes, including less frequent preeclampsia with severe features and fewer medically-indicated preterm births. B ACOG recommends treatment with an antihypertensive agent for pregnant women with persistent chronic hypertension and systolic BP >160 mm Hg or diastolic BP >110 mm Hg. B
If left untreated, preeclampsia can lead to significant maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality. C
Chronic hypertension (HTN): BP >140/90 mm Hg prior to pregnancy or prior to 20 weeks of gestation.

Gestational HTN: BP >140 mm Hg systolic or >90 mm Hg diastolic, or both, on 2 occasions at least 4 hours apart developing after 20 weeks of gestation with a previously normal BP. Gestational hypertension resolves within 6 weeks of delivery and is unaccompanied by proteinuria. ACOG notes that gestational hypertension is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes and may not represent a separate entity from preeclampsia. In addition, up to half of women with gestational hypertension will eventually develop proteinuria or other end-organ dysfunction consistent with preeclampsia.

Preeclampsia: ACOG defines preeclampsia as is a disorder of pregnancy associated with new-onset hypertension (as listed for gestational hypertension), which occurs most often after 20 weeks of gestation and frequently near term.

Preeclampsia without severe features: BP >140 mm Hg systolic or >90 mm Hg diastolic, or both, on 2 occasions at least 4 hours apart OR systolic BP of 160 mm Hg or more or diastolic blood pressure of 110 mm Hg or more AND accompanied by proteinuria (>300 mg in 24 hours or protein/creatinine ratio >0.3 mg/dL or 2+ on dipstick if quantitative methods are unavailable). In the absence of proteinuria, preeclampsia can be diagnosed by new-onset hypertension with at least one of the following: platelet count <100,000 x 109/L, renal insufficiency (serum creatinine concentrations >1.1 mg/dL or a doubling of serum creatinine concentration in the absence of other renal disease), impaired liver function (or liver transaminases elevated to twice normal concentration), pulmonary edema, or new-onset headache unresponsive to medication and not accounted for by alternative diagnoses or visual symptoms.

Preeclampsia with severe features: BP >160 mm Hg systolic or >110 mm Hg diastolic on 2 occasions at least 4 hours apart (unless antihypertensive therapy is initiated before this time) platelet count <100,000 x 109/L, elevation of LFTs to more than twice normal values or severe persistent right upper quadrant or epigastric pain unresponsive to medications, serum creatinine >1.1 dL (or a doubling of baseline creatinine), pulmonary edema, new headache unresponsive to medication and not accounted for by alternative diagnoses, and visual disturbances.
Chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia: hypertension diagnosed prior to 20 weeks of gestation with subsequent proteinuria or other signs of pre-eclampsia developing after 20 weeks.

Hemolysis, Elevated Liver Enzymes, and Low Platelet Count (HELLP) Syndrome: a severe form of preeclampsia characterized by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) elevated to 600 IU/L or more, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) elevated more than twice the upper limit of normal, and platelet count <100,000 x 109/L. HELLP syndrome primarily presents in the third-trimester, however, in 30% of cases, it is first expressed or progresses postpartum and in 15%, there is no evidence of hypertension or proteinuria.

Eclampsia: new-onset tonic-clonic, focal, or multifocal seizures in the absence of other causative conditions such as epilepsy, cerebral arterial ischemia and infarction, intracranial hemorrhage, or drug use. Up to one third of women with eclampsia do not have signs of preelampsia before seizure onset.

Preeclampsia: 3% to 7% in nulliparous women, 0.8% to 5% in multiparous women, 14% in twin gestation, and 18% in those with prior pre-eclampsia. Using US national hospital discharge survey datasets from 1980 to 2010, the incidence of preeclampsia was 3.4% among pregnant women. Rates of severe pre-eclampsia increased 6.7 fold from 1980 to 2003. Smoking, obesity and changes in diagnostic criteria had some influence on rates.

HELLP: In a Canadian population-based cohort study of over 1 million mothers with a singleton hospital live birth or stillbirth, the incidence of HELLP was 2.5 per 1000 (n = 2663). Risk factors included age ≥35 years, rural residence, nulliparity, parity ≥4, pre‐pregnancy and gestational hypertension and diabetes, assisted reproduction, chronic cardiac conditions, systemic lupus erythematosus, obesity, chronic hepatic conditions, placental disorders (e.g., fetomaternal transfusion) and congenital anomalies.

Eclampsia: 1 in 2000 to 3500 pregnancies (38%-53% occur antepartum, 18%-36% intrapartum, 11%-44% postpartum [the majority in the first 48 hours, but can be up to 23 days]). Based on findings for the placebo arm in several trials, eclampsia occurred in 1.9% of women with preeclampsia and 3.2% of women with severe preeclampsia.

Adult participants in the Helsinki Birth Cohort Study born in 1934 to 1944 whose mothers had preeclampsia or hypertension during pregnancy reported more frequent cognitive complaints (e.g., cognitive failure, distractibility, forgetfulness, false triggering) than adults born after normotensive pregnancies.

Authors of a systematic review found that the adjusted odds for mortality and necrotizing enterocolitis were lower in infants born prematurely to women with pregnancy induced hypertension or hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. There was no difference in any other infant outcomes.
Placental abruption and pre-eclampsia/hypertension are more commonly associated with preterm as opposed to term or post-term stillbirths.
Pre-eclampsia onset before 34 weeks' gestation is associated with an increased risk of critical heart defects. The overall risk, however, is low (16.7 per 1000 live births).

Maternal hypertension is associated with hypospadias - hypertension OR 1.68, 95% CI, 1.46-1.93 and preeclampsia OR 2.18, 95% CI, 1.63-2.91, based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 papers.

A prospective cohort study in Norway identified 980,560 children born at term, of whom 28,068 (2.9%) were exposed to preeclampsia. Children of women with preeclampsia were at increased risk of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.18), autism spectrum disorder (aOR, 1.29), intellectual disability (aOR 1.50), and epilepsy (adjusted OR, 1.50; 95%CI, 1.16-1.93), There was a trend for an association between preeclampsia and cerebral palsy (aOR, 1.30; 95%CI 0.94-1.80).

Unknown; genetic predisposition. In one study, the T allele of the angiotensinogen gene was associated with an increased risk of developing preeclampsia/eclampsia. In a metaanalysis, the methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase gene C677T polymorphism was associated with pre-eclampsia in most populations studied.

In a genome-wide association meta-analysis of European and Central Asian mothers, authors identified sequence variants associated with preeclampsia at ZNF831/20q13 and FTO/16q12 and at the BP variants MECOM/3q26, FGF5/4q21 and SH2B3/12q24.
Several mechanisms have been proposed:

Abnormal trophoblast invasion leading to incomplete conversion of the spiral arterioles into uteroplacental arteries and resulting in increased resistance in the placental vascular bed, vascular endothelial damage and increased platelet activation and clotting activity.
Immune maladaptation or an exaggerated maternal inflammatory response to deported trophoblasts.

One study reported different placental abnormalities in women with preeclampsia based on gestational age at onset. Findings more often associated with preeclampsia beginning early vs. late in the third trimester were hypoplasia and histological evidence of placental vascular lesions leading to insufficiency.

In a study of 200 women with preeclampsia and 200 control women, women with preeclampsia had higher levels of circulating microRNA-206, involved in gene silencing, and lower levels of endothelin-1, a potent vasoconstrictor. In another study, authors concluded that miRNAs may be antiangiogenic factors affecting endothelial cells in preeclampsia.

Among women with chronic hypertension, whose who experienced preeclampsia had lower first-trimester concentrations of both placental growth factor and antiangiogenic soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1.

list.listitem: The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommendations (USPSTF, 2023) support screening for preeclampsia in pregnant women with BP measurements throughout pregnancy. B
Screening for hypertension and symptoms of preeclampsia should occur at each prenatal visit. C
Calcium supplementation during pregnancy reduces the risk of high blood pressure, pre-eclampsia, and preterm birth. A

Low-dose aspirin shows benefit in preventing preeclampsia in high-risk women but is not recommended routinely or for primary prevention in low-risk women by the USPSTF. A The USPSTF (2021) and ACOG (2020) recommend use of low-dose aspirin (81 mg/d) as preventive medication after 12 weeks of gestation for women who are at higher risk for preeclampsia.
Vitamin D level of >50 ng/mL in Caucasian and non-obese women at high risk for pre-eclampsia was associated with a reduction in SGA risk.
Lifestyle interventions, particularly weight control, reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia. B

For women with mild chronic hypertension (defined as at least 2 blood pressure measurements, taken at least 4 hours apart and before 20 weeks' gestation, of 140 mm Hg to 159 mm Hg systolic or 90 mm Hg to 104 mm Hg diastolic without antihypertensive medication), treatment to a blood pressure of <140/90 mm/Hg was shown in a recent RCT to result in better maternal outcomes including less frequent preeclampsia with severe features and fewer medically-indicated preterm births. B

Screening for preeclampsia should occur at each prenatal visit. Screening should include measurement of BP and review of symptoms including headache, vision changes, epigastric or RUQ abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, and edema of the hands or face.

Although the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) supports screening for pre-eclampsia in pregnant women with BP measurements throughout pregnancy, no study directly compares the effectiveness of preeclampsia screening in a screened population vs. unscreened population.
The usefulness of risk factors for identification of women at risk of pre-eclampsia appears very limited.

Maternal biomarkers (e.g., placental growth factor, vascular endothelial growth factor, soluble endoglin) or serum markers (e.g., alpha fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotrophin) for early identification of preeclampsia do not appear sufficiently accurate for use in clinical practice. ACOG agrees that screening for preeclampsia using biochemical and/or biophysical markers or ultrasound in low-risk women is associated with very low positive predictive values ranging from 8% to 33% and is not likely useful.

However, in one multicenter cluster randomized clinical trial (RCT), knowledge of test results for maternal serum placental growth factor, with targeted increased surveillance for women with levels <100 pg/mL, was associated with an earlier diagnosis of pre-eclampsia and fewer severe maternal adverse events (4% vs. 5%; adjusted odds ratio 0.32; 0.11 - 0.96). There were no differences in newborn outcomes.

In addition, in a recent prospective study of first trimester screening in 5170 pregnant women, combining maternal factors with uterine artery Doppler, BP, and pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A was useful in predicting preeclampsia. The c-statistic, a measure of diagnostic accuracy/discrimination, was higher for early (0.95 [0.94-0.98]) vs. late (0.71 [0.66-0.76]) preeclampsia.

In an Italian study, screening unselected nulliparous women at 11-13 weeks of gestation using the ASPRE algorithm which combines maternal factors (mean arterial pressure, uterine artery pulsatility index and maternal serum pregnancy-associated plasma protein-A and placental growth factor) was moderately useful in predicting preterm preeclampsia with an area under the curve of 0.659 and a positive likelihood ratio of 3.74.

Authors of a 2025 Cochrane review concluded that calcium supplementation appears to make little difference in the risk of pre-eclampsia (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.67-1.04), maternal death (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.06-1.83), or preterm delivery (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.65-1.05). This updated review also found no benefit in severe maternal morbidity, perinatal loss, or stillbirth. The 2025 review updates previous evidence that found moderst benefit to calcium supplementation daily during pregnancy to reduce the risk of high blood pressure (12 trials, 15,470 women: RR 0.65; CI, 0.53-0.81), pre-eclampsia (13 trials, 15,730 women: RR 0.45; CI, 0.31-0.65), and preterm birth (11 trials, 15,275 women: RR 0.76; CI, 0.60-0.97). The effect was greatest for women with low baseline calcium intake and among those selected as being at high risk. The risk of HELLP syndrome was increased (2 trials, 12,901 women: RR 2.67; CI, 1.05-6.82) but the authors concluded that the benefit outweighs the risk.

In a more recent meta-analysis of 27 studies, with 28,492 pregnant women, authors concluded that calcium supplementation was associated with a lower incidence of preeclampsia (RR 0.51, 95% CI, 0.40-0.64) and gestational hypertension (RR 0.70, 95% CI, 0.60-0.82). Calcium supplementation reduced preeclampsia risk in both high-risk and low-risk populations. There were insufficient data to determine an ideal dose and there was significant study heterogeneity (I2 = 65%).
In a meta-analysis of 9 trials, low-dose calcium supplementation (<1 g daily) starting no later than 20 weeks' gestation also reduced the risk of pre-eclampsia.

In an RCT, pre-pregnancy calcium supplementation in women with a history of pre-eclampsia with pregnancy intentions did not reduce the risk of recurrent pre-eclampsia (RR 0.80, 95% CI, 0.61-1.06); all participants received calcium after 20 weeks' gestation. This was confirmed in another RCT of 1355 women with previous preeclampsia or eclampsia who received either 500 mg daily of calcium or placebo prior to pregnancy. In this trial, 298 of 678 in the intervention group and 283 of 677 in the placebo group had pregnancies carried beyond 20 weeks' gestation and preeclampsia re-occurred in 23% and 29%, respectively, RR 0.80, 95% CI, 0.61-1.06.

ACOG does not endorse use of calcium supplementation for reducing risk of preeclampsia because they do not think this has been sufficiently demonstrated in trials in the United States or other high resource countries.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of calcium supplementation concluded that that benefit may be overestimated. The authors reported substantial heterogeneity between studies, and found that most of the benefit was seen in the three largest trials and restricted to patients from countries with low calcium intake.
The USPSTF (2021) recommends use of low-dose aspirin (81 mg/d) as preventive medication after 12 weeks of gestation in women who are at high risk for preeclampsia.

ACOG concurs with use of low-dose aspirin, starting between 12 and 28 weeks of gestation (preferably before 16 weeks) for women with any high-risk factors for preeclampsia (previous pregnancy with preeclampsia, multifetal gestation, renal disease, autoimmune disease, type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic hypertension) and those with more than one of the moderate-risk factors (first pregnancy, maternal age of 35 years or older, BMI of more than 30, family history of preeclampsia, sociodemographic characteristics, and personal history factors).

Antiplatelet agents, largely low-dose aspirin of 75 mg or less, reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia by 17% (absolute risk reduction [ARR] 0.8%-1.7%; NNT 72; 95% CI, 52-119). The benefit is more pronounced in high-risk women (ARR 5.2%, NNT 19). Aspirin also decreased the risk of preterm birth by 8% (NNT 72; 95% CI, 52-119), neonatal death by 14% (NNT 24; 95% CI, 131-1666), and risk for small-for-gestational-age (SGA) babies (ARR 0.6%; NNT 167).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 20 trials using at least 100 mg daily from no later than 16 weeks gestation to prevent pre-eclampsia also found a reduced risk of placental abruption and antenatal hemorrhage.

In the most recent trial of 1620 women at higher risk of pre-eclampsia based on a validated screening algorithm, 150 mg of aspirin daily initiated at 11 to 14 weeks' gestation decreased the risk of preterm pre-eclampsia from 4.3% in the placebo group to 1.6% in the aspirin group (adjusted OR 0.38; 95% CI, 0.20-0.74; NNT 38).

Additional meta-analyses also support a reduction in preeclampsia risk with low-dose aspirin; in one, using 60 to 100 mg daily beginning in the second trimester and in the other with daily aspirin initiated before 16-weeks gestation.

However, in a retrospective cohort study of 457 women with chronic hypertension of whom 70% were prescribed low-dose aspirin, the overall incidence of superimposed preeclampsia was not significantly different (34.3% for those offered aspirin vs. 35.5% in those not offered aspirin). There was a significant decrease in superimposed preeclampsia without severe features (21.7% vs. 31.0%) but an increase in superimposed preeclampsia with severe features (12.6% vs. 4.4%).

listitem.strong: Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) and other antithrombotics

list.listitem: LMWH may prevent recurrent placenta-mediated pregnancy complications including pre-eclampsia, birth of a SGA newborn, placental abruption, or pregnancy loss at >20 weeks. In a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs with 358 women, fewer women given prophylactic LMWH had these recurrent outcomes compared with women not given LMWH (18.7% vs. 42.9%).

The addition of enoxaparin to aspirin vs. aspirin alone was associated with a lower frequency of a composite outcome (at least one of pre-eclampsia, abruptio placentae, birthweight <5th percentile, or fetal loss after 20 weeks) in a study of 224 women with previous severe pre-eclampsia (8.9% vs. 25%; hazard ratio 0.32; 95% CI, 0.16-0.66).

Antenatal antithrombotic therapy (heparin alone or in combination with dipyridamole triazolopyrimidine), also reduced the risk of pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and infant birthweight but offered no benefit for the primary outcomes perinatal mortality, preterm birth less than 34 weeks' gestation, and childhood neurodevelopmental handicap. In an RCT of 120 women with preterm preeclampsia, administration of recombinant human antithrombin did not prolong pregnancy (5 days [range, 0-75] vs. 6 days [range, 0-85] for the placebo group) or improve neonatal or maternal outcomes.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs showed that first-trimester initiation of micronized progesterone (400 mg twice daily) moderately reduced the incidence of HDP (RR 0.7; 95% CI 0.5-0.9; 2 RCTs with 443 participants) and preeclampsia (RR 0.6; 0.4-0.9; 3 RCTs with 5267 participants). Initiation after the first trimester did not demonstrate benefit and there is uncertainty about the extent to which these results are generalizable to pregnant individuals without risk factors for preterm birth.

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that preeclampsia may be reduced with higher intakes of omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, via supplement or food such as a fish (20 randomized controlled trials, 8306 women; RR 0.84; 95% CI, 0.69-1.01).

Authors of a second meta-analysis confirmed that n-3 fatty acids supplementation reduced risk of preeclampsia (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.70-0.97; 14 trials, I2 = 19% [no significant heterogeneity]) but not pregnancy-induced hypertension (RR 0.98; 95% CI, 0.90-1.07; 10 trials). Results for reducing preeclampsia were similar when considering only trials of low-risk women (RR 0.75; 95% CI, 0.62-0.92; 8 trials).

Antenatal antioxidants, primarily vitamins C and E, or folic acid do not reduce the risk of preeclampsia. A 2010 study found no benefit from vitamin C or E for prevention of pregnancy-induced hypertension or related adverse outcomes. However, the combination of medical food-bars containing L-arginine plus antioxidant vitamins (but not vitamins alone) reduced the risk of preeclampsia over placebo with an absolute risk reduction of 0.17 (95% CI, 0.12-0.21).
Linoleic acid 450 mg plus calcium 600 mg reduced the risk for preeclampsia by 24% in one small study of 89 women (NNT 4).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 7 trials of vitamin D vs. no supplement found evidence of reduced risk of preeclampsia, low birthweight and preterm birth with supplementation. In the 6 trials examining vitamin D with calcium, there was a lower risk of preeclampsia with combined supplementation vs. no intervention (RR 0.51; 95% CI, 0.32-0.80) but an increased risk of preterm birth (RR 1.57; 95% CI, 1.02-2.43).
Among 164 vitamin-D deficient women in Saudi Arabia, supplementation with 4000 IU of D3 compared with 400 IU reduced the risk of preeclampsia (1.2% vs. 8.6%) and intrauterine growth retardation.

In an RCT including 2408 pregnant women with a gestational age <23 weeks and a known or new diagnosis of chronic hypertension, treatment to a blood pressure target of less than 140/90 mm/Hg was associated with better maternal outcomes. The primary composite outcome of preeclampsia with severe features occurring up to 2 weeks after delivery, medically-indicated preterm birth at less than 35 weeks', placental abruption, and fetal/neonatal death occurred less frequently in the active treatment group (353/1170 [30.2%] vs 427/1155 [37.0%]; RR 0.82; 95% CI 0.73 - 0.92; number needed to treat = 15; 9 - 34). Mild chronic hypertension was defined as at least 2 blood pressure measurements, taken at least 4 hours apart and before 20 weeks' gestation, of 140 mm Hg to 159 mm Hg systolic or 90 mm Hg to 104 mm Hg diastolic (without antihypertensive medication). Women in the control group were withdrawn from antihypertensive medication unless blood pressure measurements were at least 160 mm Hg systolic and/or at least 105 mm Hg diastolic.
There is insufficient evidence to determine whether nitric oxide or its precursors prevent preeclampsia.
There is insufficient evidence of benefit from diuretics in prevention of preeclampsia; given the level of adverse effects from these agents, the use of diuretics is not recommended.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend bed rest, limited activity, or increased activity to prevent preeclampsia or its complications.

In a study of 68 women, those randomized to practicing yoga three times weekly in the second trimester had significantly reduced rates of pregnancy-induced hypertension, pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes and intrauterine growth restriction cases compared with those randomized to walking.
There is also insufficient evidence that reducing dietary salt prevents pre-eclampsia.

Adherence to a DASH diet was reduced the incidence of preeclampsia in a small RCT of 85 pregnant women diagnosed with gestational hypertension and chronic hypertension – 43.2% in the intervention arm vs. 65.9% in the control arm.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 RCTs of diet and exercise interventions in overweight and obese pregnant women did not find a reduced risk of hypertensive disorders or preeclampsia although there was a positive effect on reducing pregnancy weight gain.

Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis while in labor and postpartum. The standard dose is a loading dose of 10% magnesium sulfate, 4 g by infusion pump over 10 minutes, followed by a continuous infusion of 1 to 2 g/hour (see Treatment).

In one RCT of 144 women in India, a low-dose continuous infusion (0.75 g/hour after a loading dose of 4 g) was as effective as standard dosing at preventing recurrent seizure in women with eclampsia (7.46% vs. 8.57%, respectively). In a second RCT in Nigeria, "low dose" magnesium sulfate (9 g loading dose [4 g IV and 5 g IM] followed by 2.5 g every 4 hours for 24 hours post-delivery or post last fit) was comparable to usual dose (14 g followed by 5 g every 4 hours) for women with eclampsia.

In a Chinese RCT of 788 women with previous preeclampsia, there were no differences between women randomized to pre-pregnancy 4 mg folic acid vs. 0.4 mg for recurrent preeclampsia (10.2% vs. 9.8%, RR 0.96, 95% CI, 0.76-1.19) or gestational hypertension (63.2% vs. 64.3%, RR 1.01, 95% CI, 0.85-1.18). However, the incidence of early-onset (12.7% vs. 19.3%) and severe preeclampsia (9.8% vs. 16.9%) were significantly lower in the high-dose group. Adherence was >80% in 74.1% and 73% of women, respectively.

list.listitem: Preeclampsia without severe features: BP >140 mmHg systolic or >90 mm Hg diastolic, or both, on 2 occasions at least 4 hours apart OR systolic BP of 160 mm Hg or more or diastolic blood pressure of 110 mm Hg or more AND accompanied by proteinuria (>300 mg in 24 hours or protein/creatinine ratio >0.3 mg/dL or 2+ on dipstick if quantitative methods are unavailable).

Preeclampsia with severe features: BP >160 mmHg systolic or 110 mm Hg diastolic on 2 occasions at least 4 hours apart (unless antihypertensive therapy is initiated before this time), platelet count <100,000, elevation of liver function tests to more than twice normal values or severe persistent right upper quadrant or epigastric pain unresponsive to medications, serum creatinine >1.1 mg/dL (or a doubling of baseline creatinine), pulmonary edema, new headache unresponsive to medication and not accounted for by alternative diagnoses, and visual disturbances.
Additional criteria for other hypertensive disorders in pregnancy are listed in the section on definitions.

BP should be measured in a seated or semi-reclined position so that the arm used is at the level of the heart. If blood pressure is measured in the lateral recumbent position, the readings may be falsely low.

Symptoms that raise suspicion for preeclampsia include headache (50%-75% of patients), vision changes such as blurred vision or scintillating scotoma (19%-32% of patients), epigastric or RUQ pain, rapid weight gain, and edema.
In a systematic review, the most useful symptoms for predicting complications in women with preeclampsia were headache, epigastric pain, and visual disturbances.
Blood pressure as noted above. (Note that higher blood pressure is not correlated with increased seizure risk; a person can seize with a normal BP.)

Urinary protein >300 mg in 24 hours or protein/creatinine ratio >0.3 mg/dL or 2+ on dipstick if quantitative methods are unavailable. (Note that the amount of proteinuria is expected to increase over time with expectant management and this change is not predictive of perinatal outcome.)

A 24-hour urine collection is the gold standard for quantification of urinary protein; proteinuria is part of the diagnostic criteria. Authors of a recent systematic review, however, found that a 12-hour urine collection compared favorably with a 24-hour urine collection for the diagnosis of proteinuria in women with suspected pre-eclampsia.
CBC with platelets, serum creatinine, LDH, AST and ALT are obtained to evaluate for end-organ involvement and to diagnose patients with severe preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome.

Urinary protein to creatinine ratio values <150 mg/g have a good negative predictive value, especially for severe proteinuria; for values >150 mg/g, a 12- or 24-hour urine should be collected, because the sensitivity for significant proteinuria is only fair and the correlation with a 24-hour urine is not consistent across studies.

In a systematic review of the accuracy of a spot protein:creatinine ratio for detecting proteinuria in pregnant women with hypertension, a negative result was useful in ruling out proteinuria of 0.3 g/day or more (LR− 0.21). In an Australian study, this test was found to be highly correlated (r = 0.98) with a 24-hour urine protein collection with a positive predictive value of 94% and a sensitivity of 95% for predicting proteinuria.

Uric acid lacks sensitivity and specificity as a diagnostic tool and is a poor predictor of complications of pre-eclampsia but may be helpful in identifying women with chronic HTN who will develop preeclampsia.
Ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid index (AFI) should be performed if pre-eclampsia is suspected to evaluate for IUGR and oligohydramnios.

ACOG concluded in their most recent committee opinion that taking a detailed medical history to evaluate for risk factors is currently the best and only recommended screening approach for pre-eclampsia.

In the most recent bulletin on preeclampsia, ACOG noted that screening for preeclampsia using biochemical and/or biophysical markers or ultrasound in low-risk women was associated with very low positive predictive values ranging from 8% to 33% and is not likely useful.

Potential predictors of pre-eclampsia under consideration include serum biomarkers (e.g., inhibin A, plasma factor VII, plasma-associated plasma protein A), urinary biomarkers (e.g., fibrinogen alpha chain), and/or second-trimester uterine artery Doppler pulsatility index. D-dimer is also under investigation as a diagnostic tool, as increased plasma d-dimer is associated with pre-eclampsia in the third trimester.
Fibrinogen, measured in the third trimester using a cutoff of 2.87 g/L or less, was predictive of pre-eclampsia in one study with an AOC 0.87.

Low placental growth factor (PIGF), an angiogenic factor associated with placental dysfunction, has a high sensitivity and negative predictive value for development of pre-eclampsia within 14 days among women with suspected pre-eclampsia (AOC 0.87). Authors of a meta-analysis of 40 studies with 3189 cases of preeclampsia and 89,498 controls found an overall predictive odds ratio of a positive test of 9, 95% CI, 6-13. In another study, first-trimester PlGF was the best biomarker for early onset pre-eclampsia. Among low risk women, a single PIGF performed at 14-16 weeks gestation was less useful. A change in PIGF along with other biomarkers from first to early second trimester may be more predictive. A randomized controlled trial of revealed vs. concealed PIGF testing in women with suspected pre-eclampsia showed a shorter median time to diagnosis of pre-eclampsia in the group whose PIGF results were revealed: 1.9 days vs. 4.1 days (time ratio = 0.36, 95% CI, 0.15-0.87), and a lower incidence of maternal adverse outcomes (4% vs. 5%; adjusted OR = 0.32, 95% CI, 0.11-0.96).

NICE (2019) recommends offering PlGF-based testing to help rule out preeclampsia in women presenting with suspected preeclampsia (for example, with gestational hypertension) between 20 weeks and up to 35 weeks of pregnancy.

Increased asymmetric dimethylarginine and homocysteine levels were found one month prior to the onset of pre-eclampsia in a study of 252 women; the group of women with no complications had constant levels throughout pregnancy. In another study, first trimester nuclear magnetic resonance-based metabolomic analysis, including arginine and 2-hydroxybutyrate, was useful in predicting pre-eclampsia (Area under the curve [AUC] 0.84; 95% CI, 0.77-0.94). Adding uterine Doppler pulsatility index improved the model (AUC 0.916; 95% CI, 0.836-0.996).

Hypertriglyceridemia is associated with and precedes the onset of pre-eclampsia among pregnant women. Vitamin D deficiency of <20 ng/mL is also associated with pre-eclampsia (OR 2.78; 95% CI, 1.45-5.33).
See for a recommended approach to diagnosis and treatment.
For women with preeclampsia, planned delivery from 34 weeks' onward reduced a composite outcome of maternal morbidity.

Antihypertensive treatment for women with mild to moderate hypertension during pregnancy prevents severe hypertension and appears to reduce the risk of preeclampsia and maternal morbidity. There is concern that such treatment may decrease placental perfusion and lead to growth restricted fetus over time. B

Delivery of the infant is the only cure for pre-eclampsia/eclampsia. The decision for early delivery vs. medical management of early pre-eclampsia with severe features must be made on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the gestational age at diagnosis and fetal and maternal complications. C

Early delivery for women with early-onset severe preeclampsia appears to reduce neonatal morbidity; for women with preeclampsia without severe features, early planned delivery appears to reduce maternal morbidity but increases neonatal morbidity with no increase in neonatal mortality. B Authors of a recent meta-analysis of participant level data, including 1790 patients with preeclampsia from 6 trials, found planned delivery from 34 weeks' onward reduced a composite outcome of maternal morbidity. ACOG (2020) recommends delivery at 37 weeks for women with stable preeclampsia without severe features and at 34 weeks in preeclampsia with severe features unless other indications for delivery arise or neonatal survival is not anticipated. B
Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia and for initial treatment of eclampsia. A
Steroids are effective in reducing infant morbidity and mortality between 24 and 34 weeks of gestational age and should be given. A
ACOG recommends antihypertensive therapy for pregnant women with persistent chronic hypertension and systolic BP >160 mm Hg or diastolic BP >105 mm Hg.

NICE (2010) recommends stopping antihypertensive treatment in women with chronic hypertension taking angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers if they become pregnant, due to increased risk of congenital anomalies, and offering alternatives. Thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics are also associated with increased risk.

NICE (2019) recommends offering antihypertensive treatment to pregnant women who have chronic hypertension and who are not already on treatment, or to women with gestational hypertension or preeclampsia, if they have sustained systolic blood pressure of 140 mmHg or higher or sustained diastolic blood pressure of 90 mmHg or higher. They recommended target BP is 135/85 mm Hg or less. They recommend antihypertensive treatment for all women with BP of 160/110 mm Hg or more (see severe hypertension below).

There is insufficient evidence to recommend antihypertensive treatment of mild to moderate BP elevations <160/110 mm Hg. While antihypertensive treatment reduces the risk of severe hypertension (RR = 0.49, 95% CI, 0.40-0.60; NNT 10), there is no influence on the development of pre-eclampsia (RR = 0.92, 95% CI, 0.75-1.14) and no reduction in neonatal mortality (RR = 0.72, 95% CI, 0.50-1.04) or preterm birth (RR = 0.96, 95% CI, 0.83-1.12).

Authors of a Cochrane review found that beta-blockers were better than methyldopa for reducing the risk of severe hypertension. A separate metaanalysis of trials of oral beta-blockers confirmed the reduction in risk of severe hypertension but there were no substantive benefits for mother and/or baby, and beta-blockers were associated with an increase in small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants (RR 1.36, 95% CI, 1.02-1.82; 12 trials). Beta-blocker exposure, however, in the first trimester of pregnancy is associated with a small increased risk of cardiovascular defects, cleft lip/palate, and neural tube defects.

A 2025 network meta-analysis found treatment of gestational HTN with labetolol resulted in lower rates of pre-eclampsia (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.28-0.87) and prematurity (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.52-0.90) compared with treatment with nifedipine. Blood pressure control was similiar with nifedipine, methyldopa, and labetolol.

Authors of a 2020 network meta-analysis of oral antihypertensives from 14 RCTs and 8 cohort studies with 4464 women with chronic hypertension also found a higher risk of SGA infants with atenolol; use of nifedipine or methyldopa was associated with significantly lower placental abruption rates (OR 0.29, 95% CI, 0.15-0.58 and 0.23, 95% CI, 0.11-0.46, respectively) and severe hypertension; no agent significantly affected the incidence of preeclampsia.

There is insufficient evidence to determine how tightly hypertension should be controlled. In the CHIPs trial of 987 women with diastolic BP 90-105 mmHg (74.6% with pre-existing hypertension), there were no significant differences with tight (target diastolic BP 85 mm Hg) vs. less tight control (target diastolic BP 100 mmHg) for pregnancy loss, high-level neonatal care, adverse perinatal outcomes, or overall maternal complications. Women in the less-tight contro groupl had a higher frequency of severe maternal hypertension (≥160/110 mm Hg) than those in the tight control group (40.6% and 27.5%, respectively)

Use of magnesium sulfate reduces risk of eclampsia (RR 0.41; CI, 0.29-0.58; NNT 100); however, side effects are common, most often hot flashes (number needed to treat to harm [NNH] = 6). Risk of placental abruption is also reduced (RR 0.64; CI, 0.50-0.83), but there is a small increase in risk of cesarean section (5%). A

Serious adverse effects of magnesium sulfate (respiratory depression and cardiac arrest) result from its action as a smooth muscle relaxant and occur at high doses (respiratory depression at 12 mg/dL [10 mEq/L] and cardiac arrest at 30 mg/dL [25 mEq/L]. Loss of deep tendon reflexes occur at a serum magnesium level of 9 mg/dL (7 mEq/L) and monitoring their presence helps to avoid these serious adverse effects.
Magnesium sulfate also reduces the risk of eclampsia compared with phenytoin (3 trials, 2291 women; RR 0.08; CI, 0.01-0.60) and nimodipine (1 trial, 1650 women; RR 0.33; CI, 0.14-0.77).
For women with eclampsia, magnesium sulfate reduces the risk of maternal death (7 trials; 1396 women; RR 0.59; CI, 0.38-0.92) and recurrent seizures (7 trials; 1390 women; RR 0.43; CI, 0.33-0.55). A

Magnesium sulfate also reduces seizure recurrence more effectively than phenytoin (RR 0.34; CI, 0.24-0.49). Maternal mortality differences were not statistically significant, but magnesium decreased the risk of pneumonia, need for ventilation, admission to the intensive care unit (ICU), and decreased neonatal ICU admissions (RR 0.73; CI, 0.58-0.91) over phenytoin. A

Magnesium sulfate is preferred in women with eclampsia compared with a lytic cocktail (usually chlorpromazine, promethazine and pethidine); magnesium sulfate reduced the risk of maternal death (RR 0.14; CI, 0.03-0.59), recurrent seizures (RR 0.06; CI, 0.03-0.12), and of serious maternal morbidity.

Some studies have suggested that use of magnesium sulfate does not affect disease progression, mode of delivery, or maternal/fetal adverse effects in pre-eclampsia without severe features and therefore should be used only to prevent seizure in pre-eclampsia with severe features or in treatment of eclampsia. B

Dosing : There is insufficient evidence to support a preferred regimen for magnesium sulfate administration. The usual regimen in the United States is intravenous (IV) administration of a 4 to 6 g loading dose over 20 to 30 minutes, followed by a maintenance dose of 1 to 2 g/hour (1 g/hour if mild renal failure).

In a small RCT of 37 obese women with preeclampsia, use of a 6 g IV loading dose followed by a 2 g/h IV maintenance dose more reliably achieved therapeutic serum magnesium concentrations (at least 4.8 mg/dL) compared to a 4 g IV loading dose followed by a 1 g/h infusion. It is not clear that reaching this target level is clinically meaningful.

Use of dexamethasone for thrombocytopenia in HELLP syndrome did not lead to any difference in overall maternal morbidity or mortality but did lead to a greater increase in platelet count at more than 48 hours, decreased number of hospital days, and increased mean time to delivery. There were no differences in perinatal morbidity or mortality, but birth weight was increased in the dexamethasone group.

Steroids are effective in reducing neonatal morbidity and mortality in infants between 24 and 34 weeks gestation. Steroids can be considered in late preterm infants (34-37 week) but can lead to an increase in neonatal hypoglycemia.

Acute onset of severe elevations of systolic BP >160 mm Hg and/or diastolic BP >110 mm Hg should be treated with antihypertensive agents for a goal SBP of 140 to 160 mm Hg and DBP of 90 to 110 mm Hg. Intravenous hydralazine or labetalol or oral nifedipine are most commonly used (see ).
In one RCT, labetalol and nifedipine were similarly effective.

Emergency consultation from maternal–fetal medicine, internal medicine, anesthesia, or critical care subspecialists should be obtained if the BP threshold is still exceeded after one of these protocols.

Authors of a Cochrane review found limited data on comparative effects of antihypertensive agents for very high blood pressure in pregnancy. Calcium channel blockers vs. hydralazine or magnesium sulfate reduced persistent high blood pressure. The authors advised selection based on the clinician's experience with a particular drug and the adverse effect profile, avoiding diazoxide, ketanserin, nimodipine (higher risk of eclampsia) and magnesium sulphate for treating hypertension.
In a recent trial of 60 women with acute hypertensive emergency in pregnancy (BP 160/110 mm Hg or greater), IV hydralazine and oral nifedipine were equally effective in lowering of blood pressure.

In a small RCT of 60 women with a sustained increase in systolic blood pressure of 160 mm Hg or higher or diastolic blood pressure of 110 mm Hg or higher, oral nifedipine lowered blood pressure more quickly than did intravenous labetalol.
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers should not be used due to risk of fetal malformations.
There is insufficient evidence to determine whether garlic is effective in preventing preeclampsia.
Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to support use of guided imagery for hypertension in pregnancy.
In an RCT of 253 women with preeclampsia, adjunctive phytosterol+nifedipine vs. nifedipine+placebo resulted in a shorter time to control BP but no differences in maternal or neonatal outcomes.

The only known cure for pre-eclampsia/eclampsia is delivery of the infant. The decision to intervene with early delivery vs. the practice of expectant management in early severe pre-eclampsia must be made on a case-by-case basis, taking into account gestational age at the onset of disease and potential fetal and maternal complications.

American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology 2020 guidelines list the following conditions as precluding expectant management:
Maternal: Uncontrolled severe-range blood pressures (persistent systolic blood pressure 160 mm Hg or more or diastolic blood pressure 110 mm Hg or more not responsive to antihypertensive medication); persistent headaches, refractory to treatment; epigastric pain or RUQ pain unresponsive to repeat analgesics, visual disturbances, motor deficit or altered sensorium; stroke; myocardial infarction; HELLP syndrome; new or worsening renal dysfunction (serum creatinine greater than 1.1 mg/dL or twice baseline); eclampsia, or suspected acute placental abruption or vaginal bleeding in the absence of placenta previa. Fetal: Abnormal fetal testing, fetal death or without expectation for survival at the time of maternal diagnosis (e.g., lethal anomaly, extreme prematurity), persistent reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery.

Authors of a Cochrane review of early delivery vs. expectant management for women with severe pre-eclampsia at 24 to 34 weeks' gestation found insufficient data for maternal outcomes, including maternal death, eclampsia, pulmonary edema, HELLP syndrome, and stroke. There was little difference in incidence of caesarean section (6 studies, 745 women; RR = 1.01 for the interventional group, 95% CI, 0.91-1.12). An interventional approach showed increased neonatal morbidity, including intraventricular hemorrhage (RR 1.94, 95% CI, 1.15-3.29) and respiratory distress (RR 1.50, 95% CI, 1.11-2.02). Neonatal mortality was not significantly different (3 studies, 343 women; RR 1.11, 95% CI, 0.62-1.99).

Based on 4 small trials, expectant management vs. intervention for women with severe early-onset pre-eclampsia is associated with lower neonatal morbidity (e.g., intraventricular hemorrhage, hyaline membrane disease, prematurity); larger studies are needed.

However, in a Latin American RCT of 267 women with severe pre-eclampsia from 28 to 34 weeks, there were no differences in perinatal mortality or morbidity between expectant vs. prompt delivery. In this trial, there were higher rates of SGA infants and abruption with expectant management.

Authors of a meta-analysis of participant level data, including 1790 patients with preeclampsia from 6 trials, found planned delivery from 34 weeks' onward reduced a composite outcome of maternal morbidity defined as one or more of the following: death, eclampsia, stroke, pulmonary edema, HELLP syndrome, and placental abruption (2.6% for planned delivery vs 4.0% for expectant management; adjusted RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.36 - 0.98). For neonates, there may be a decreased risk of small for gestational age at birth, and an increase in short-term respiratory morbidity. The difference in gestational age at birth was a mean of 4 days. Rates of vaginal birth were not different.

A randomized open-label trial of induction vs. expectant monitoring for women with gestational hypertension or mild pre-eclampsia after 36 weeks gestation found fewer women with a poor maternal outcome among women in the induction group vs. expectant group (31% vs. 44%) but no differences in eclampsia or neonatal death. A British RCT also found lower costs for a similar group of women randomized to induction vs. expectant management, primarily due to antenatal costs for the latter group.

Planned early delivery in women with mild late preterm hypertensive disorders was associated with poorer parent-reported neurodevelopmental outcomes in their children at 2 years of age based on follow-up of 330 women (47% of the original cohort) who participated in the Hypertension and Preeclampsia Intervention Trial at near Term (HYPITAT-II) trial. This difference did not persist when the children reached 5 years of age.

In a multicenter study of women with preeclampsia or chronic hypertension with superimposed pre-eclampsia conducted in 46 maternity units in the United Kingdom, planned delivery at 34 to 36 6/7 weeks' gestation vs. expectant management up to 37 weeks’ gestation resulted in more favorable outcomes for mothers; adverse maternal outcomes occurred in 65% vs. 75% (adjusted RR 0.86; 95% CI, 0.79-0.94). Half (54%) of the women randomized to expectant management were induced prior to 37 weeks. Adverse maternal outcome was defined as a composite of progression to severe preeclampsia and many other possible morbidities related to the central nervous system; cardiorespiratory, hematological, hepatic, and renal systems; and placental abruption. Although more neonates were admitted to a neonatal special care nursery in the planned delivery group, there was no increase in neonatal morbidity.

list.listitem: In an open-label trial of 352 women with non-severe gestational hypertensive disorder and gestational age of 34 to 37 weeks conducted at 51 centers in the Netherlands, immediate delivery was associated with an increase in neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (5.7% vs. 1.7%; number needed to treat to harm 25) compared with expectant management until at least 37 weeks' gestation. Expectant management, however, was associated with a statistically non-significant increase in a composite of adverse maternal outcomes, which included thromboembolic complications.

For pregnant patients with mild chronic hypertension, data from a retrospective cohort analysis of an RCT conducted for another purpose suggested that planned delivery before 39 weeks’ gestation did not improve maternal outcomes or composite of severe neonatal outcomes. The study fell short of concluding that waiting until 39 completed weeks for planned delivery is clearly superior and RCTs are needed to address this question.
New dietary salt restriction is not recommended; there is insufficient evidence for ongoing salt restriction in women with pre-existing hypertension.
In one small RCT of 60 women with severe pre-eclampsia, carbetocin (an oxytocin agonist) was as effective as oxytocin in preventing postpartum hemorrhage.
Hospitalize if preeclampsia with severe features, HELLP syndrome, eclampsia, or if preeclampsia without severe features and unreliable patient, poor access to care, or worsening disease.
Once preeclampsia with severe features is diagnosed, the patient should be referred to a high-risk OB specialist in a tertiary care facility with adequate ICU and neonatal resources.

Magnesium toxicity can occur rapidly, especially in the setting of acute renal failure. It is therefore important to monitor reflexes, mental status, and respiratory status of the patient. See Table 1

If magnesium toxicity is suspected, stop the infusion and check serum magnesium level. If there is somnolence or respiratory depression, stop the infusion and administer 1 g calcium gluconate IV over 3 minutes.

Eclampsia [38%-53% antepartum, 11%-44% postpartum (usually within 48 hours)]: use supportive measures (e.g., prevention of aspiration, call for help) and treat with a 2 g bolus of magnesium sulfate if the patient is already receiving magnesium infusion. If not, load with 4 to 6 g of magnesium sulfate IV over 20 minutes and then continue the infusion at 1-2 g/h.

In cases refractory to magnesium sulfate (still seizing at 20 minutes after the bolus or more than two recurrences), ACOG, 2020 suggests use of sodium amobarbital (250 mg IV in 3 minutes), thiopental, or phenytoin (1,250 mg IV at a rate of 50 mg/minute).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 studies concluded that none of the pooled estimates were able to accurately predict or rule out eclampsia, with moderate specificity (83-94%) and poor sensitivity (29-56%).

If left untreated, pre-eclampsia can lead to both maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality in the form of seizures, pulmonary edema, acute renal failure, thrombocytopenia, HELLP syndrome, DIC, placental abruption, oligohydramnios, fetal growth restriction, and fetal distress. C
The earlier in pregnancy pre-eclampsia occurs, the higher the risk of significant complications. A

If severe pre-eclampsia is diagnosed before 24 weeks of gestation and left untreated, perinatal survival is only 6.7%. Maternal morbidity is 27% and includes HELLP syndrome (20%), placental abruption (13%), and eclampsia (6.7%).

If diagnosed at >24 weeks but <27 weeks of gestation, perinatal survival is 35% and neonatal complications include respiratory distress syndrome (RDS; 84%), intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH; 71%), bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD; 19%), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC; 16%), and seizures (16%).

With treatment, patients diagnosed with severe pre-eclampsia at >24 weeks but <27 weeks of gestation have an infant survival rate of about 76%. Rates of RDS, IVH, NEC, and seizures decreased by 24%, 30%, 7%, and 11%, respectively, and infants spent an average of 35 fewer days in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) than their untreated counterparts. Maternal complications were similar between groups (e.g., 13% HELLP, 5%-6% placental abruption, 3%-7% thrombocytopenia).

Treatment for women between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation with conservative management vs. immediate delivery allowed for an additional 2 weeks of completed gestation with significant improvements in outcomes; rates of RDS, NEC, and admission to the NICU decreased by 29%, 5%, and 9%, respectively. Infants spent an average of 16 fewer days in the NICU. Maternal complications and infant rates of BPD and IVH were similar.

In one large population-based Canadian study, women with HELLP syndrome vs. women without the syndrome had a 10‐fold higher maternal mortality (95% CI 1.6–84.3), elevated severe maternal morbidity (9.6 versus 121.7 per 1000), higher perinatal mortality (4.3 vs. 21.0 per 1000) and higher perinatal mortality/severe neonatal morbidity (21.2 vs. 202.4 per 1000).

ACOG 2020 guidelines recommend weekly evaluation of platelet count, serum creatinine, and liver enzymes in women with gestational hypertension or preeclampsia without severe features, and more often if suspecting disease progression. Monitor BP and symptoms using in-office and ambulatory approaches; weekly office visits are suggested. During labor and immediately after delivery, monitor BP and symptoms.
NICE 2019 also has specific guidelines for follow-up and monitoring based on severity of disease.

Magnesium sulfate should be continued for 12 to 24 hours postpartum. Clinical factors (e.g., BP stabilization, symptom resolution, diuresis) may be used to guide the length of postpartum magnesium therapy.
For post-delivery pain, ibuprofen vs. acetaminophen does not appear to increase BP in women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy based on two small RCTs.
Postpartum blood pressure (BP) is highest three to six days after birth. However, there are no data to guide treatment for these women.

Patients can have seizure activity up to 3 to 4 weeks postpartum. They have to be cautioned about this at discharge and instructed to report any new or worsening symptoms of pre-eclampsia as well as any BPs >160/105 mm Hg.

Women with a history of pre-eclampsia are at risk of pre-eclampsia and preterm birth in a subsequent pregnancy, particularly if the index pregnancy delivered preterm. Rates of recurrence vary from 5.9% (vs. 0.8% in control women) up to 50% (the latter if index preterm delivery complicated by pre-eclampsia).

However, in a recent meta-analysis of 22 studies, if the hypertensive disorder recurred, in general it was milder with respect to maximum diastolic BP, proteinuria, the use of oral antihypertensive and anticonvulsive medication, the delivery of a small-for-gestational-age child, premature delivery, and perinatal death.

Hypertension: Women with hypertension in pregnancy are at risk of subsequent hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. In a large cohort study, the risk of subsequent hypertension was 5.31 (range: 4.90-5.75) after gestational hypertension, 3.61 (range: 3.43-3.80) after mild pre-eclampsia, and 6.07 (range: 5.45-6.77) after severe pre-eclampsia. The risk of subsequent type 2 diabetes mellitus was 3.12 (range: 2.63-3.70) after gestational hypertension and 3.68-fold (range: 3.04-4.46) after severe pre-eclampsia.

Heart disease: Recent preeclampsia may be a teachable moment for cardiovascular risk reduction. In a 9-month clinical trial, Heart Health 4 Moms, including 151 U.S. women with preeclampsia within 5 years, women in the intervention arm reported significantly greater knowledge of CVD risk factors, increased self-efficacy for healthy eating although no difference in DASH diet adherence, and less physical inactivity than controls, although reported physical activity did not differ between groups. The intervention included online educational modules, a community forum, and communication with a lifestyle coach and the control group internet links to CVD risk reduction information.
A higher percentage of women with peripartum cardiomyopathy had pre-eclampsia compared to the general population (22% vs. about 5%).

Kidney disease: Women with pre-eclampsia are also at higher risk of end-stage renal disease (4.7 after a first pregnancy [95% CI, 3.6-6.1] and 6.7 after a second pregnancy [95% CI, 4.3-10.6]), although the overall risk is small (overall rate, 3.7 per 100,000 women per year).

This association was confirmed using the Taiwan's National Health Insurance Research Database of over 13,000 women, and in a meta-analysis of 21 studies with 110,803 cases with and 2,680,929 controls without preeclampsia (RR 6.35, 95% CI, 2.73-14.79). In the Taiwan study, the hazard ratio (HR) was highest among women with a history of pre-eclampsia superimposed on chronic hypertension (HR 44.72; 95% CI, 22.59-88.51). Women with gestational hypertension had a higher risk of end-stage renal disease than did women without pregnancy-associated hypertensive disorders (HR 5.82; 95% CI, 2.15-15.77).
Depression: Women with pre-eclampsia or HELLP may have a higher risk of subsequent depression.

Children and young adults born to mothers with pre-eclampsia have a slightly increased systolic (2.39 mm Hg) and diastolic (1.35 mm Hg) blood pressure and body mass index (0.62 kg/m2) than children without this history.

There appears to be an increased risk of stroke in offspring of women with pre-eclampsia; in 1 study, the crude hazard ratio for stroke among people whose mothers had pre-eclampsia was 1.9 (95% CI, 1.2-3.0).

cell.label: Pre-eclampsia suspected: BP >140/90, proteinuria, symptoms or rapid weight gain
Pre-eclampsia laboratory tests: CBC with platelets, serum creatinine, LDH, AST, ALT, and 24-h urine for protein. Assess fetus: NST, BPP
Gestational hypertension: If >20 weeks of gestation, elevated BPs, normal laboratory tests, and urine protein <300 mg in 24 h

If NST and AFI are reassuring, continue expectant management with increased surveillance. Weekly NST, BPP, laboratory tests. Repeat above testing for change in status (increase in BP, new or worsening proteinuria, or new symptoms). Ultrasound every 3 to 4 weeks for growth. Plan delivery in the 37th week if stable
Pre-eclampsia without severe features: BPs >140/90 but <160/110 and urine protein >300 mg OR symptoms/abnormal labs
Noncompliant patient, poor access to care, or disease progression?
If near term, consider amniocentesis for fetal lung maturity. Deliver if mature

If remote from term: • Give steroids • BP, laboratory tests, and 12-24-h urine protein weekly to twice weekly • Ultrasound for fetal growth every 3-4 weeks • NST/BPP weekly to twice weekly • Instruct patient to report any symptoms (e.g., headache, visual changes, abdominal pain, swelling) • Plan for delivery at 37 weeks unless other indications for delivery occur

Indications for delivery: • Pulmonary edema in mother • Progressive deterioration in hepatic or renal function • Persistent CNS symptoms (e.g., headache, vision changes, mental status changes) • Eclampsia • Persistent epigastric or RUQ pain or nausea/vomiting • Placental abruption • Non reassuring fetal status (e.g., IUGR, oligohydramnios, abnormal NST, BPP, or umbilical artery Doppler) • Platelets <100,000 • Severe hypertension despite 2 oral medications

• Plan for induction/delivery within 24 h • Magnesium sulfate is optional (4-6 g bolus then 1-2 g/h) watch for toxicity: monitor reflexes and mental status) • Monitor labs every 8-12 h • Monitor fluid balance (strict intake/output) • Treat SBPs >160, DBPs >105
Pre-eclampsia with severe features: BP >160/110, symptoms, OR abnormal labs (see Diagnostic criteria)
Offer termination: Fetal survival 6.7%, maternal morbidity 27%

• Admit to tertiary care hospital • Magnesium sulfate 4-6g load then 2-3 g/h • Steroids • Daily laboratory tests and fetal monitoring (NST/ BPP) • Treat BP with up to 2 oral medications to keep BP 140-160/90-100 • Ultrasound for growth every 3 weeks • Monitor for vaginal bleeding (abruption) • Plan for delivery at 34 weeks unless other indications for delivery occur
